meta.title: Who really said "Anyone who doesn't believe in miracles is not a realist"? | Quotle.info
meta.description: Not Audrey Hepburn. The line is David Ben-Gurion's, documented in a 1973 book on Israel (a 1956 CBS-interview variant is reputed but unverified) — a paraphrase of his remark about Israel.
meta.ogTitle: Who really said 'Anyone who doesn't believe in miracles is not a realist'?
meta.ogDescription: Not Audrey Hepburn — it's David Ben-Gurion's line about Israel, documented in a 1973 book (a 1956 CBS-interview variant is reputed but unverified).

answer.label: Not Audrey Hepburn — actually David Ben-Gurion
answer.authorDates: 1886–1973 · Zionist statesman & first Prime Minister of Israel
answer.sourceLine: Audrey Hepburn never said this. The thought is David Ben-Gurion’s, spoken about the founding of Israel. Wikiquote documents it as “With us, anyone who doesn’t believe in miracles isn’t a realist” (attributed to him in Roman Frister, Israel: Years of Crisis, Years of Hope, 1973, p. 45); a reputed variant, “In Israel, in order to be a realist you must believe in miracles,” is credited to a CBS interview of 5 October 1956 ↗ that Wikiquote flags as unverified. The smoothed, context-free wording popular online is a later paraphrase.

source.excerpt: In Israel, in order to be a realist you must believe in miracles.
trail: Wikiquote files the line under Audrey Hepburn’s Misattributed section ↗, crediting it instead to David Ben-Gurion.

The David Ben-Gurion page ↗ sources “With us, anyone who doesn’t believe in miracles isn’t a realist” to Roman Frister’s 1973 book Israel: Years of Crisis, Years of Hope (p. 45), and marks the 1956 CBS-interview variant ‘not in citation given’ (i.e. unverified).
Goodreads carries the exact line under Ben-Gurion’s name with a ‘misattributed-audrey-hepburn’ tag ↗.
source.excerptNote: The popular “Anyone who doesn’t believe in miracles is not a realist” strips away Ben-Gurion’s specific reference to Israel; that exact wording appears attributed to him in Charles A. Garfield’s Psychosocial Care of the Dying Patient (1978).
source.rightsNote: The idea is firmly David Ben-Gurion’s, attributed to him in a 1973 book on Israel (with a reputed but unverified 1956 CBS-interview variant) — but the exact wording that circulates under Hepburn’s name is a smoothed paraphrase with no single canonical first-publication, so no clean copyright status can be asserted for it.

author.name: David Ben-Gurion
author.heading: About David Ben-Gurion
author.metaLine: 1886–1973 · Zionist statesman & first Prime Minister of Israel
author.bio: David Ben-Gurion led the Zionist movement in Mandatory Palestine and, on 14 May 1948, proclaimed the establishment of the State of Israel, becoming its first prime minister and defense minister. He guided the new state through the 1948 war and its early nation-building years. His remark that Israelis must believe in miracles to be realists captured his sense of the country’s improbable birth and survival.

cite.sourceCitation: David Ben-Gurion, attributed in Roman Frister, Israel: Years of Crisis, Years of Hope (1973), p. 45 (“With us, anyone who doesn’t believe in miracles isn’t a realist”); a variant reputedly from a CBS interview of 5 October 1956 is unverified. Exact wording “Anyone who doesn’t believe in miracles is not a realist” attributed to Ben-Gurion in Charles A. Garfield, Psychosocial Care of the Dying Patient (New York: McGraw-Hill, 1978).

misattribution.heading: How Audrey Hepburn got the credit
misattribution.intro: This is a classic feel-good misattribution: an inspirational one-liner pinned to a beloved star it has nothing to do with. The words are David Ben-Gurion’s, spoken about the improbable survival of the state of Israel.

items.why: Quote sites, memes and jewelry blogs routinely stamp the line on Hepburn’s image, but Wikiquote places it in her Misattributed section ↗ with no source from her lifetime.

The founding Prime Minister of Israel said it of his young country — “With us, anyone who doesn’t believe in miracles isn’t a realist” — as attributed to him in a 1973 book on Israel ↗ (a reputed 1956 CBS-interview variant is unverified).

misattribution.truthLine: The line is David Ben-Gurion’s reflection on Israel, not Audrey Hepburn’s — documented in a 1973 book on Israel ↗ (a reputed 1956 CBS-interview variant is unverified), and absent from anything Hepburn is known to have said.

context.heading: Why he said it
lead: Ben-Gurion’s line is not a greeting-card sentiment about optimism — it is a hard-nosed political observation. He was describing a state that came into being against enormous odds and had to keep defying them to endure. For him, treating the miraculous as a normal working assumption was realism.

Stripped of “In Israel” and re-captioned over a photograph of Audrey Hepburn, the sentence becomes a soft inspirational platitude — which is exactly how it now spreads, and exactly why the original meaning is lost.
